Assuming you can get into a well regarded university and are interested in a 'real' major (science, engineering, mathematics, and so on), absolutely. The biggest con about college is without doubt the money. Beyond that it's an absolutely huge benefit. In no particular order here are some reasons why:

  • Breadth of knowledge. I come from a CS/mathematics background but even before university I already knew how to code to a rather high standard even compared to most graduates. However, I still learned an immense amount in college on topics I would have never studied on my own simply because they did not particularly interest me at the time. For instance abstract automata theory is about as exciting as watching paint dry, yet it's the fundamental basis of all artificial intelligence. My educational background enables me to easily peruse the latest literature on advances in artificial intelligence and actually understand what's going on. In some post I made on Voat a while back I was able to code a basic AI learning system without any trouble at all. You can't predict where the world is going to be in 10 years. Having a breadth of knowledge prepares you for the future.

  • Cliche time! Some of the most important lessons will be learned outside the classroom. I'm not even referring to social things. Going to a top tier university will mean you get access to some amazing resources you won't have access to anywhere else. For instance I was given free reign on a supercomputer in a multi million dollar audio-visual lab. I didn't really realize how incredible an opportunity this was at the time. You'll also get access to some of the leading brains in the field you're interested in. Going out and having drinks with a researcher responsible for a key development in my field of study? Pretty bad ass and not something that's going to happen anywhere else. Having a systems engineering class taught by a guy who was leading the R&D on the 'future' (whoops!) of computing? Yip! Even the student body. You'll be around other students who are comparable to yourself in terms of... "intrinsic educational motivation and competence"... shall we say.

  • Fun. In the end we're born, go to school for 20 years, work for 50 years, retire for 15 years, then die. College is fun, a whole lot of fun. It shouldn't be your primary motivation given the money involved, but 4 (...or more) years of incredible fun is a pretty nice notch on the belt when looking back at your life. It's also a great opportunity to meet the person you might end up spending the rest of your life with.

  • Life results. I have some atypical views here so I'm not going to hit on this too much, but under current socioeconomic conditions you are extremely unlikely to find a desirable job without a degree. A degree itself is also far from a guarantee although the connections you make in and through college do definitely go a long ways towards providing some sort of guarantee. To put it one way, you are certainly more likely to be able to monetize yourself proportional to your merit with a degree than without.

I don't know where you're from, but I'll give you my experience from the US. We have public community colleges (junior colleges) here. They award 2 year associate's degrees. They consist of freshman/sophmore level classes and are dramatically cheaper that 4 year universities.

I would suggest getting an AS in mathematics. You'll take 3 semesters of calc, diff eq, and possibly dsicrete math or linear algebra. For your science/lab courses take 2 semesters of calc based physics. If you like the experience you'll be in good shape to pursue a BSc in any STEM field. If you don't, then you won't be out a lot of money and there are decent paying skilled trade jobs that you can pursue. I've met too many people who went to college for the sake of going to college. They bought in to the 'go to college, get a good job' schtick. That transborder studies degree isn't impressing anyone. Just keep in mind that degrees are ubiquitous. Some jobs require them just to weed out the applicant pool.

College is worth it if you are srudying stem or you got into an elite college. The elite college is worth it even if you aren't srudying stem because you can make relationships that are very hard to make elsewhere.

College can be very worthwhile if you're not wasting your time and money on courses that won't take you anywhere in life. Best advice I could give to you is go to a community college first, get your general coursework out of the way, and figure out what you want to do with your life job wise. Once you know what you want to do, then you can decide if you need to go to a university.

It is if you pick the right area of study. Do some research before you go into debt studying art history or some other thing that will not allow you to get a job when you are through. Just to toss out a suggestion, RN with an entry level of AS Nursing will pay well with less time and money up front and really good job prospects.

Where it is from doesn't matter. Grades don't even matter. Just that you made it through. This has been my experience. I have a BS in Construction Management and work in that field (although I couldn't find a job right away). Third year working in CM and I make 75k a year. I live in CT though and it's stupid expensive to live here.

If there is a specific interest or field you want to enter (especially STEM fields), it is definitely worth it. If you are going just to go, then not so much.

Also if you do go, I suggest attending a community college to get all the core stuff done and transfer. You would save a lot of money and get basically the same quality of education

Go take tours of local community colleges, and tech schools. Stay away from for-profits if possible.

Look into doing something with your hands that you find interesting, and can't be outsourced - welding, carpentry, HVAC, plumbing, etc.

I'm a massage therapist. I sleeve $15k on school, but went to a fire profit that closed, and now I can't get copies of my transcripts or a diploma, so I'm not paying my student loans to be petty. I am not in a position to need credit, so I'm fine with that.

Massage is great, but find something that really interests you! That's why tech schools are so fun, you get to really do things and immediately know what kind of job you are going to have. I'm not saying that white collar degrees don't do things, I'm just saying you could get a degree in accounting/sales and end up doing something totally unrelated anyways.

In the long run, it is worth it. The college degree has lost some of its cache from 20 or 30 years ago. It's considered the new high school diploma since most people have one. Well, most whites not from the Deep South.

A liberal arts degree is definitely questionable now as to its worth. You almost need a Master's, MBA, or graduate degree in a profession to validate it. However, in some cases, you might need your undergraduate degree to even apply to a graduate program unless you have professional experience which can substitute it.

It really depends on what you want to do it life. If you like the law or medicine and want to be a lawyer or doctor or engineer, then you need an undergrad degree. Then another post graduate degree. ;) This is what your career guidance counselor is for. Just a real truth: Rarely do people follow their high school career aspirations all the way through to their 20s. Things change. Values change. Financial situations change. Priorities change.

Figure out what you want to do and then pursue it with all your heart. If what you want to do includes tertiary education then you're off to college. Otherwise you're not.

In case it's not clear figuring out what you want to do is the important question here. So if you're serious about your future then don't waste your time and energy on social media and video games. Instead get out and start racking up some useful life experiences. How else can you decide what you want to do unless you have some information to base that decision on?

Ok, guy... I went to one of the "best" American colleges. I have a terminal degree from a "prestigious" school. I've worked in universities. My opinion might be relevant, since there's a decent chance you'd take a class from someone like me. Bear in mind, I don't know anything about you.

1) There's no advantage in being stupid. Don't willfully think, "I'm better than college. I stuck it to the man. I've got a job making $172,000 a year. Suck it, college boy." Most of the richest people in the world did NOTHING for their money. Money isn't everything. There's always someone richer than you, and it does NOT mean he's better, more experienced, more insightful. It's strikingly akin to being tall.

2) That being said, you're right to focus on money. My dad listened to various college administrators (salesmen) explain loan packages. His conclusion? "It's hardly worth being white if you're in debt." That's some of the truest insight I've ever heard. It's true about mortgages, too. If you have to work to pay someone else, you're a slave. And your complaints are the whine of a slave.

3) So is it worth it? It can be good. Most of the people in this thread are right about deciding what you're good at and what you want to do. Junior college, taking one or two classes at a time while you work, anything to reduce cost is a good idea.

4) Education doesn't always lead to a degree. Howard Hughes was a great aviation engineer (and born rich). He "went" to universities -- he never stayed to complete a degree, but he didn't begrudge the research. Suppose you want to take a class on circuits. If you know the material, you can enroll in just that class. If you're great at it, the professors will want to work with you. I was friends with multiple PhD students in the Ivy League who did not hold undergraduate degrees. (Mainly math students who had struck gold on a paper or two...)

Which leads us back to "there's no advantage in being stupid".

So... what do you want to do? What do you like?
